transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. Before we get started, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in to see me today?

Um… mostly work stuff. I keep getting up from my station when I’m supposed to stay there, or I’ll pop up in meetings before I even realize I’m doing it. My supervisor said it’s turning into a safety issue because I just kind of take off without thinking.

Right before you get up or leave your seat, do you notice an inner feeling of restlessness or an urge that builds up and pushes you to move, or does it just happen suddenly without any warning sensation?
Yeah… I do feel it first. Like if I’m standing by the machine or sitting in training, it’s like this pressure building up in me. I just need to move or stretch or go do something right then.
Are you currently taking, or have you recently started, any new medications—especially antipsychotics or anti-nausea drugs—around the time these urges to move began?
Um… I don’t think so. I haven’t really started anything new like that, at least not that I know of.
Have you noticed this kind of restlessness and urge to get up and move since childhood or adolescence, or is this something that started more recently, say within the past few weeks or months?

It’s been around a long time. Like, even in elementary school I was always getting in trouble for not staying in my seat… talking over the teacher, blurting stuff out. They’d send notes home because I’d wander around the room.
Do you also struggle with staying focused on tasks, following through on details, or often losing track of things, even when you're not moving around?

Yeah… I do. Like with inventory logs or those CNC training pages, I’ll try to focus, but after a few minutes it’s like the numbers or words just blur together. Then I realize I didn’t really take it in and have to go back over it.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of both hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (inability to stay seated, urge to move, blurting out, wandering) and inattentive symptoms (losing focus on detailed tasks, needing to reread material, difficulty sustaining attention). Symptoms are pervasive across settings (school historically, now workplace) and cause functional impairment (workplace safety concerns, supervisor complaints). No recent medication changes (e.g., antipsychotics) to suggest drug-induced akathisia, and the chronic developmental course argues against an anxiety-based restlessness disorder. This combination of longstanding inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms meeting criteria in multiple domains supports ADHD, combined presentation.
